plaibox.tip: Now test the plain version on three real citizens before publishing.

modules.d: Ethical, lawful use of AI in campaigns, advocacy and civic mobilisation.
modules.body:
AI in campaigns: efficiency and responsibility

Campaigns and advocacy organisations use AI to draft speeches and messages, segment audiences, translate materials, plan events, coordinate volunteers, analyse polling and draft fundraising appeals. These uses can make smaller campaigns more competitive. They also raise serious risks: deceptive content, privacy violations, manipulation and breaches of election law. Responsible campaigns win trust as well as votes.

Know the rules

Election and campaign laws differ by country and change frequently. They may govern campaign finance, spending limits, disclosure of sponsorship, silence periods before voting, use of state resources, voter data and political advertising. Increasingly, laws address AI and synthetic media in political content. The European Union's regulation on transparency and targeting of political advertising imposes labelling and transparency requirements and restricts targeting using sensitive personal data; several U.S. states have enacted laws requiring disclosure of, or restricting, deceptive AI-generated election content; and electoral management bodies in many countries issue codes of conduct. In Cameroon and elsewhere, follow the electoral code and the guidance of the electoral authority. When uncertain, seek legal advice before launching AI-generated content.

Red lines for ethical campaigns. ① No deepfakes or synthetic content depicting real people saying or doing things they did not. ② No fabricated endorsements, quotes or statistics. ③ No deceptive impersonation of officials, election bodies or opponents. ④ No content designed to suppress voting or mislead people about when, where or how to vote. ⑤ Clear disclosure of AI-generated content where required by law or platform policy, and as good practice.

Voter data and privacy

Political opinions are sensitive personal data under many data protection laws. Collect only what you need, with a lawful basis; secure it; respect individuals' rights; and do not buy or use data obtained unlawfully. AI-driven microtargeting that exploits psychological vulnerabilities or sensitive characteristics raises legal and ethical concerns, as shown by the Cambridge Analytica controversy.

Legitimate high-value uses

  • Drafting and translating policy explainers in multiple languages.
  • Producing speeches and talking points from the candidate's or organisation's own positions.
  • Summarising polling and research into briefings.
  • Planning field operations and volunteer schedules.
  • Drafting accessible materials for people with disabilities.
  • Monitoring public conversation for misinformation about your campaign.
  • Testing message clarity with diverse audiences.

Advocacy and civil society campaigns

Advocacy organisations use AI to analyse legislation, draft petitions and submissions, mobilise supporters and tell stories of affected people. The same ethical standards apply: truthful claims, consent for personal stories, transparency about funding and authorship, and respect for opponents' dignity.

Fundraising communications

AI can personalise fundraising appeals, but avoid manipulative urgency and false claims, comply with donation rules (sources, limits and reporting), and honour unsubscribe requests and data protection rights.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my campaign compliance and communications advisor. I will describe my campaign or advocacy goal and country. Help me identify the legal rules I must verify (finance, advertising, data, AI disclosure, silence periods), draft a code of conduct for AI use with clear red lines, and produce three message drafts based only on the positions and facts I provide — flagging anything that needs verification or disclosure.

📚 Glossary

  • Microtargeting: tailoring messages to small audience segments using personal data
  • Voter suppression: efforts to discourage or prevent eligible people from voting
  • Silence period: pre-election period restricting campaigning in some countries
  • Disclosure: labelling AI-generated or sponsored political content

📖 References

  • European Union — Regulation (EU) 2024/900 on the transparency and targeting of political advertising.
  • International IDEA — resources on electoral integrity and AI.
  • U.K. Information Commissioner's Office — guidance on political campaigning and data protection.
  • National electoral codes and electoral management body guidance (verify for your country).

quiz.q: A Cameroonian candidate's team wants an AI-generated audio clip of a rival 'admitting' to corruption, labelled as satire in small print. What is the correct judgement?
opts: Acceptable if the satire label appears clearly at the start of the clip
A red line: synthetic content of a real person saying things they did not say
Acceptable if shared privately with volunteers in closed groups rather than on public pages
Acceptable if the corruption claims are already in published reports
quiz.x: Deepfakes depicting real people saying or doing things they did not are a red line; small-print labels do not stop the clip being shared as real. A clear label is the runner-up, but audio clips travel without labels.

quiz.q: A campaign in an EU country wants to target ads at voters inferred to be of a particular religion. Under the EU political advertising regulation, what is the key concern?
opts: It restricts targeting using sensitive personal data such as religion
It bans online political ads in the last 30 days before any EU vote
Religion-based ads require approval from the national election body first
Targeting is fine if the ad discloses the sponsor and spending amount
quiz.x: Regulation (EU) 2024/900 restricts targeting based on sensitive personal data and imposes labelling and transparency requirements. Disclosure alone does not cure prohibited targeting.

quiz.q: A party's data team in Nairobi is offered a voter list with phone numbers and inferred ethnicity, scraped from a leaked database. What should they do?
opts: Decline it; data obtained unlawfully should not be bought or used
Use it if the party's lawyer signs off on the scraping method used
Use it after checking that the numbers are still active and correct
Use the phone numbers but discard the ethnicity column before importing
quiz.x: The module says not to buy or use unlawfully obtained data. Removing the ethnicity column is a tempting half-measure, but the phone numbers are tainted by the same unlawful source.

quiz.q: A US state candidate wants to use an AI-generated image of herself at a factory she visited, recreated because the real photos were blurry. What is the best approach?
opts: Ask the factory owner for written permission and then post it unlabelled
Use it in printed leaflets, where AI disclosure laws do not apply
Use it unlabelled, since it depicts a real event involving the candidate
Check state law and platform rules and disclose that the image is AI-generated
quiz.x: Several US states require disclosure of AI-generated election content and platforms have their own rules; disclosure is good practice anyway. Depicting a real event does not make a synthetic image authentic.

quiz.q: An advocacy NGO in Lagos uses AI to turn interviews with flood victims into campaign stories. What safeguard is essential?
opts: Letting the AI add emotional details to strengthen each victim's story
Changing names, but keeping vivid details so the stories still feel real
Obtaining consent for each personal story and keeping claims truthful
Publish aggregate figures instead, since stories tend to risk privacy
quiz.x: Advocacy must have truthful claims and consent for personal stories. Changing names without consent is insufficient, and AI-added details make stories untrue.

quiz.q: A campaign's AI-drafted text message says 'Polls in your area close at 4 pm' when they close at 6 pm. It was an error. What is the issue and response?
opts: The provider's fault; report the AI tool to the electoral commission
Potentially voter-suppressing; correct it immediately and review the process
A legal risk if it is proven that turnout fell in the affected area
Minor error; correct it in the next scheduled message to the same list
quiz.x: Misleading people about when to vote touches a red line even if unintended, so rapid correction and process review are needed. Waiting for the next scheduled message lets the harm happen.

quiz.q: A small opposition party in Cameroon, with limited staff, asks which AI use offers high value with low risk. Which is best?
opts: Creating synthetic crowd photos to show the strength of the movement
Writing opinion polls and publishing projected results to motivate voters
Building psychological profiles of undecided voters from social posts
Generating volunteer schedules and field plans for weekend outreach
quiz.x: Planning field operations is listed as a legitimate high-value use. Fabricated polls, synthetic crowds and psychological profiling raise truthfulness, deception and privacy concerns.

quiz.q: A campaign fundraising email drafted by AI says 'Only 2 hours left or we lose the race!' Nothing is actually due. What does the module advise?
opts: Avoid manipulative false urgency and keep fundraising claims accurate
Allowed if a human staffer approved the final wording before sending
Allowed if the email also includes a clear unsubscribe link at the end
Allowed, since urgency messaging is common across all campaign fundraising
quiz.x: Fundraising should avoid manipulative urgency and false claims. An unsubscribe link and human approval are good practice but do not make a false claim acceptable.

quiz.q: Days before polling, a campaign wants to post AI-generated videos, but the country has a 48-hour campaign silence period. Which action is most appropriate?
opts: Post during the silence period if the videos avoid naming the candidate
Check the electoral code and authority guidance on what silence periods cover
Post before the silence period starts and leave the content online
Post during the silence period from supporters' personal accounts rather than official pages
quiz.x: Silence-period rules differ by country and may cover existing content or third parties; check the electoral code and seek advice when uncertain. Posting earlier and leaving it up may or may not comply.

quiz.q: A campaign's AI microtargeting tool proposes sending fear-based messages to people its model flags as anxious about crime. What is the main issue?
opts: Fear-based messages are less effective than hopeful ones in most studies
Microtargeting is permitted for parties above a set size threshold
Exploiting psychological vulnerabilities raises legal and ethical concerns
The model's anxiety predictions may be inaccurate for a share of voters
quiz.x: Microtargeting that exploits psychological vulnerabilities raises legal and ethical concerns, as in the Cambridge Analytica controversy. Inaccuracy is a lesser issue; the practice is problematic even if accurate.

facts.t: EU regulation on the transparency and targeting of political advertising.
facts.more: It requires labelling and transparency notices and restricts targeting based on sensitive personal data. It is a sign of where electoral regulation is heading worldwide.

facts.t: Facebook users whose data Facebook said may have been improperly shared with Cambridge Analytica.
facts.more: Facebook's own 2018 estimate. The case made voter-data microtargeting a global regulatory and ethical issue.

facts.t: The module's ethical red lines for AI in campaigns.
facts.more: No deepfakes of real people, no fabricated endorsements or statistics, no impersonation, no voter suppression, and clear AI disclosure where required or as good practice.

facts.t: Political opinions are a sensitive data category under many data-protection laws, including the GDPR.
facts.more: Processing them needs a specific lawful basis and stronger safeguards. Campaigns should collect only what they need and never use unlawfully obtained lists.

labs.title: Go, check first, or red line?
labs.intro: A campaign team in Cameroon proposes these AI uses. Sort each one.
items: Translate the candidate's published manifesto into Pidgin and Fulfulde
Summarise last month's polling into a two-page briefing
Run AI-written SMS ads on the day before voting
Target ads by inferred religion using a purchased data list
Make an AI video of a rival 'admitting' to corruption as satire
Send WhatsApp messages saying opposition voters vote on Monday
Use AI-generated images of crowds in campaign posters
Draft volunteer shift schedules for polling-day transport
labs.tip: Silence periods, disclosure rules and data law vary by country. When unsure, get legal advice before launch.

labs.title: Campaign compliance vocabulary
labs.intro: Match each term to the practice it describes.
pairs: Tailoring messages to small segments using personal data
Discouraging eligible people from casting a ballot
A window before polling when campaigning is restricted
Telling audiences that content is AI-made or sponsored
The legal ground that permits processing a voter's data
Electoral body's rules that parties commit to follow
labs.tip: Knowing the vocabulary helps you ask your lawyer the right questions.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the final campaign week
plaibox.intro: You coordinate communications for a civic advocacy coalition in a national campaign. Scoring: 2 = best practice, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.

steps.s: A volunteer shares a convincing AI audio clip of a rival leader insulting a region.
o: Hold it and check source and provenance first
Unverified audio could be synthetic. Sharing it could make you a vector of disinformation.
Share it with a note that it is 'unconfirmed'
Labels don't stop harm. You would amplify a possible deepfake.
Ignore it and say nothing internally
You don't spread it, but you miss the chance to document and report it.

steps.s: A data broker offers a list of 200,000 phone numbers tagged by ethnicity.
o: Buy it but use only the phone numbers, not addresses
Better than ethnic targeting, but the list's lawful origin and consent are unknown.
Decline and build lists from people who opted in
Political and ethnic data is sensitive. Opt-in lists respect the law and voters.
Buy it: other campaigns are already using such lists
Unlawfully obtained sensitive data creates legal and ethical exposure.

steps.s: The team wants an AI-generated photo of 'supporters at a rally' for a poster.
o: Use a consented real rally photo, or label the image AI-made
Truthful imagery or clear disclosure keeps the campaign honest.
Use it unlabelled; it only illustrates the mood of the rally
Presenting synthetic crowds as real misleads voters.
Use it only in small print runs where reach is limited
Smaller reach, same deception. Disclosure is the issue, not volume.

steps.s: A donor wants personalised appeals telling people 'the country will collapse without you'.
o: Run it, but send it only to existing loyal donors who opted in
Narrower, but manipulative urgency is still the problem.
Run it: tested urgency messages reliably raise more money
False alarm and manipulation erode trust and may breach fundraising rules.
Use factual urgency tied to real deadlines and honour opt-outs
Honest, specific appeals respect donors and data rights.

plaibox.win: You protected truth, voters' data and the campaign's integrity. Responsible campaigns win trust as well as votes.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the five red lines and the voter-data rules. Check the law first, never fabricate, and never use unlawful data.

modules.d: Detecting, prebunking and responding to disinformation and synthetic media.
modules.body:
The threat

Disinformation — false information spread deliberately to deceive — threatens elections, public health, social cohesion and trust. Generative AI lowers the cost of producing persuasive false text, images, audio and video at scale. Notable cases include fabricated audio of a party leader released days before Slovakia's 2023 election, during a pre-election period when media coverage was restricted, and AI-generated robocalls imitating U.S. President Biden's voice to discourage New Hampshire primary voters in 2024, for which the political consultant behind them faced a multimillion-dollar FCC fine and criminal charges.

Distinguish the terms

Misinformation is false information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is false information spread deliberately. Malinformation is genuine information shared to cause harm, such as leaked private data. Responses differ: correcting a well-meaning misinformed citizen differs from countering a coordinated influence operation.

Verification skills

  • Source check: who published it first? Is the account new, anonymous or impersonating someone?
  • Reverse image and video search: tools such as Google Lens, TinEye and the InVID-WeVerify plugin help find earlier versions or original contexts of images and video frames.
  • Context check: is a real image being reused from another event, date or place?
  • Lateral reading: open new tabs to see what reliable sources say about the claim and the source, rather than analysing the page itself.
  • Signs of synthetic media: inconsistencies in lighting, hands, text, lip-sync or audio artefacts — though detection by eye is increasingly unreliable.
  • Provenance: content credentials based on the C2PA standard can show how content was created and edited, where publishers adopt them.
Detection tools are not verdicts. AI-detection tools for synthetic text, images and audio produce both false positives and false negatives. Use them as one signal among several — source, context, corroboration and provenance — not as proof.

Prebunking and resilience

Research on inoculation theory by Sander van der Linden, Jon Roozenbeek and colleagues shows that exposing people in advance to weakened forms of manipulation techniques — emotional language, false dichotomies, scapegoating, fake experts — improves their ability to recognise them later. Prebunking campaigns, including large-scale tests with short videos on social platforms, have shown measurable effects. Media literacy, trusted local messengers and transparent institutions build long-term resilience.

Responding effectively

  1. Assess reach and harm before responding; responding to a fringe falsehood can amplify it.
  2. Verify facts quickly with authoritative sources.
  3. Respond with the truth first — the "truth sandwich": state the fact, briefly note the falsehood, and repeat the fact.
  4. Use trusted messengers and the channels where the falsehood spreads, including WhatsApp and local languages.
  5. Report coordinated or illegal content to platforms and authorities.
  6. Document incidents for analysis and accountability.

Using AI defensively

AI can monitor public conversation for emerging narratives, cluster similar claims, draft fact-check explainers and translate corrections into multiple languages quickly. Human fact-checkers verify and decide. Respect free expression: counter falsehoods with truth and transparency rather than suppressing legitimate dissent.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my disinformation response coach. I will describe a claim, image or video circulating in my community (without personal data). Guide me through source, context and provenance checks and suggest verification tools to use. Help me decide whether and how to respond given its reach, and draft a truth-sandwich correction for WhatsApp in plain language, marking facts I must verify with authoritative sources.

📚 Glossary

  • Disinformation: false information spread deliberately
  • Misinformation: false information shared without intent to deceive
  • Prebunking: pre-emptive exposure to manipulation techniques
  • Lateral reading: checking a source by consulting other sources
  • C2PA: standard for content provenance and credentials
  • Truth sandwich: fact, brief mention of falsehood, fact again

📖 References

  • van der Linden, S. (2023). Foolproof: Why Misinformation Infects Our Minds and How to Build Immunity.
  • Roozenbeek, J. et al. (2022). Psychological inoculation improves resilience against misinformation on social media. Science Advances.
  • Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) — c2pa.org.
  • FCC (2024) enforcement action regarding AI-generated robocalls in the New Hampshire primary.
  • Wardle, C. & Derakhshan, H. (2017). Information Disorder. Council of Europe.

quiz.q: A WhatsApp message in Bamenda falsely says a clinic is closed. The sender is a worried mother who believed it. How should this be classified?
opts: Disinformation, because the content is false and is spreading widely
Misinformation, because it is false but shared without intent to deceive
Propaganda, because it affects public trust in health services
Malinformation, because it causes harm to the clinic's reputation
quiz.x: Misinformation is false information shared without intent to deceive. Spread does not make it disinformation, which requires deliberate deception; malinformation involves genuine information.

quiz.q: A leaked, genuine medical record of an opposition candidate is posted to embarrass them. Which term fits best?
opts: Political satire
Misinformation
Disinformation
Malinformation
quiz.x: Malinformation is genuine information shared to cause harm, such as leaked private data. It is not disinformation because the content is real.

quiz.q: A fact-checker in Yaounde sees a photo said to show this week's floods. Which first step is most efficient for checking whether it is recycled?
opts: Run a reverse image search to find earlier versions or original contexts
Study the lighting and shadows closely for signs that AI created the image
Ask the account that posted it to share the original file with metadata
Run it through an AI-image detector and publish the probability score
quiz.x: Reverse image search via tools like Google Lens or TinEye quickly finds earlier versions. Detectors give unreliable verdicts, and visual inspection is increasingly unreliable.

quiz.q: An AI-detection tool reports a viral audio clip of a minister is '92% likely synthetic'. A newsroom wants to headline 'Fake audio'. What is the best advice?
opts: Wait for the minister's office to confirm, then publish as their claim
Run a second detector and publish if both give scores above 80%
Treat it as one signal and corroborate with source, context and provenance
Run the headline, since 92% is above the usual 90% threshold for confidence
quiz.x: Detection tools produce false positives and negatives; they are one signal among several, not proof. A second detector adds little independence; corroboration through source, context and provenance is needed.

quiz.q: A rumour about a fake cholera cure is shared by 40 accounts with little engagement. A ministry wants to issue a national press release refuting it. What does the module suggest?
opts: Assess reach and harm first; a big response could amplify a fringe claim
Report the 40 accounts to the police for spreading false health claims about cholera
Respond at once nationally, as early rebuttal prevents any spread
Ask platforms to remove every post that mentions the supposed cure
quiz.x: Assess reach and harm before responding, because responding to a fringe falsehood can amplify it. Monitoring and preparing a correction is better than a national release.

quiz.q: A ministry drafts a correction about false fuel-price rumours. Which structure follows the 'truth sandwich'?
opts: Note the falsehood, link a fact-check article, and invite questions
Quote the rumour in full, explain why it is wrong, then state the facts
State the fact, then give a detailed timeline of how the rumour spread
State the fact, briefly note the falsehood, then repeat the fact
quiz.x: The truth sandwich leads with the fact, mentions the falsehood briefly, and repeats the fact. Leading with the rumour reinforces it.

quiz.q: An election commission wants to build resilience before a vote. Based on inoculation research, which intervention is most likely to help?
opts: Daily lists of false claims circulating, posted on the commission site
Short videos showing common manipulation techniques like fake experts
Requiring platforms to label all political content as unverified
Training officials to spot deepfakes by eye during the campaign
quiz.x: Prebunking by exposing people to weakened forms of manipulation techniques has shown measurable effects. Daily lists of false claims are reactive and may repeat falsehoods.

quiz.q: A US newsroom checks a viral claim on an unfamiliar website. Instead of studying the site's design, the reporter opens new tabs to see what others say about the outlet. What technique is this?
opts: Reverse image search
Source triangulation
Lateral reading
Provenance checking
quiz.x: Lateral reading means leaving the page to see what reliable sources say about the claim and source. Provenance checking concerns content credentials like C2PA.

quiz.q: A photo agency in Nairobi wants to help audiences verify its images. Which measure most directly supports provenance?
opts: Watermarking each photo with the agency logo before publication
Attaching C2PA-based content credentials showing creation and edits
Publishing photographers' names and contact details with each image
Releasing images in high resolution so that manipulation is visible
quiz.x: C2PA content credentials show how content was created and edited. Visible logos are easily removed and do not record edit history.

quiz.q: A civic group's AI monitor flags many posts criticising a government policy as 'disinformation'. Most are opinions. What should the group do?
opts: Raise the model's confidence threshold and report the remaining posts
Report all flagged posts to platforms, since the AI is trained on false claims
Have human fact-checkers review; respect dissent and counter only falsehoods
Stop monitoring, since AI cannot tell opinion from fact in any setting
quiz.x: Human fact-checkers verify and decide, and free expression must be respected: counter falsehoods, do not suppress dissent. A higher threshold still lets the AI decide.

facts.t: FCC fine over AI robocalls imitating President Biden before the 2024 New Hampshire primary.
facts.more: The calls urged voters to stay home. The consultant behind them also faced criminal charges, which shows voice-cloning for voter suppression carries real legal consequences.

facts.t: Misinformation, disinformation and malinformation.
facts.more: Mis = false, shared without intent. Dis = false and deliberate. Mal = genuine but shared to harm. Each needs a different response.

facts.t: Fabricated audio of a party leader circulated days before the election.
facts.more: It spread during the pre-election moratorium, when media coverage was restricted, so rebuttal was harder. Timing is part of the attack.

facts.t: An open standard for content credentials showing how media was created and edited.
facts.more: Provenance helps where publishers and devices adopt it. A missing credential proves nothing on its own, so combine it with source, context and corroboration checks.

labs.title: Mis-, dis- or malinformation?
labs.intro: Classify each case by falsity and intent.
items: An aunt forwards an old flood photo believing it shows Limbe today
A pastor shares a wrong polling date he misheard on radio
A network of new accounts posts the same fake ballot-burning video
A cloned voice of a governor announces a fake curfew
A candidate's real medical records are leaked to shame him
A journalist's genuine home address is posted to incite harassment
A page invents a 'WHO warning' about a vaccine to drive clicks
labs.tip: A well-meaning sharer needs a kind correction. A coordinated operation needs documentation and reporting.

labs.title: Respond to a viral falsehood
labs.intro: A false claim about polling stations is spreading on WhatsApp in Bamenda. Order the response.
steps: Assess reach and potential harm before deciding to respond
Run source, context and reverse-image checks
Confirm the facts with the electoral authority
Draft a truth sandwich: fact, brief falsehood, fact again
Send it through trusted local messengers in local languages
Report coordinated or illegal content to the platform and authorities
Document the incident for analysis and accountability
labs.tip: Responding to a fringe falsehood can amplify it, so assessing reach comes first.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the polling-day video
plaibox.intro: You lead a civic fact-checking desk in Yaoundé. A video 'showing ballot stuffing' is spreading fast. Scoring: 2 = best, 1 = partial, 0 = risky.

steps.s: An AI detector says the video is '92% likely authentic'.
o: Publish that the video is authentic, citing the detector
Detectors are one signal, not a verdict. They produce false negatives.
Combine source, context, reverse search and provenance checks
Corroboration across several signals is the professional standard.
Discard the detector result and wait for more reports
Ignoring a signal is safer than overtrusting it, but waiting alone doesn't verify anything.

steps.s: Reverse search finds the same footage posted in 2018 from another country.
o: Prepare a correction showing the original date and place
Context reuse is now documented. That is evidence you can show.
Post 'FAKE!' in bold with no explanation
Correct but unpersuasive. Showing the evidence builds trust.
Name the account that first shared it as a foreign agent
You can't prove intent. Accusations can defame and inflame.

steps.s: The false video is mostly circulating in Fulfulde-speaking WhatsApp groups.
o: Publish a detailed French correction on your website
Accurate, but it misses the channel and language where the harm is.
Ask platforms to remove all election videos until polls close
Overbroad. It suppresses legitimate speech.
Send a voice-note truth sandwich through trusted local messengers
Right channel, right language, trusted voice.

steps.s: A minister asks you to help 'flag opposition pages' as disinformation.
o: Agree, but only for pages you have verified as false
Narrower, but it ties your desk to one side and risks your neutrality.
Decline and apply the same evidence standard to all claims
Non-partisan, evidence-based work protects both free expression and credibility.
Agree: the government is the legal authority on this
Partisan flagging turns fact-checking into suppression of dissent.

plaibox.win: Excellent. You corroborated, showed evidence, used the right channels and stayed non-partisan.
plaibox.lose: Review the verification skills and the response principles. Detectors aren't verdicts, and corrections must be evidence-based and neutral.

modules.d: A practical playbook for responsible AI use in your institution, campaign or civic organisation.
modules.body:
Your civic AI playbook

Your capstone is a Civic AI Playbook for a government unit, legislature office, political campaign, party or civil society organisation. It should enable effective AI use while protecting citizens' rights, trust and democratic integrity.

Playbook components

  1. Context: organisation, mandate, audiences, jurisdiction and applicable laws (data protection, electoral, public administration, AI regulation).
  2. Principles: legality, accountability, transparency, equality, privacy, participation and truthfulness.
  3. Approved uses: priority use cases — for example policy research, plain-language communication, translation, casework drafting, consultation analysis, misinformation monitoring.
  4. Prohibited uses and red lines: deceptive synthetic media, fabricated claims, voter suppression, unlawful profiling, automated decisions about citizens without legal basis and human review.
  5. Data rules: handling of citizens', constituents' and voters' data; approved tools; sensitive data protections.
  6. Verification and review: sources for every fact; human review before publication; correction procedures.
  7. Transparency: when and how AI use is disclosed to the public.
  8. Disinformation response plan: monitoring, verification, response thresholds, truth-sandwich templates, trusted messengers, reporting channels.
  9. Roles and accountability: who approves uses, reviews outputs and responds to incidents.
  10. Training and review: staff training and a review schedule as laws and tools change.
Legitimacy test. For each use in your playbook, ask: if the public learned exactly how we used AI here, would it increase or decrease trust in our institution or campaign? Uses that would decrease trust need redesign or removal.

Your capstone deliverable

Submit the playbook (no more than six pages), a disinformation response template, and one worked example applying the playbook to a real or realistic scenario. Your mentor reviews it for legality, non-partisanship, practicality and democratic integrity.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as my civic AI playbook drafter. Using my organisation type, mandate and country, draft a playbook with the ten components from this module in under six pages. Apply the legitimacy test to each proposed use. Include a disinformation response template with thresholds and a truth-sandwich example, and list the laws and guidance I must verify for my jurisdiction.

Going deeper — capstone playbook: your Civic AI Playbook

A playbook is judged by whether staff under pressure — on election night, during a crisis, at a busy constituency office — would actually follow it. Write it for that moment: short decision rules, named roles and templates ready to use.

Step-by-step timeline.

  • Week 1 — Map the context. Identify the applicable laws (data protection, electoral, access to information, public administration and any AI-specific rules) and inventory current AI use in your organisation.
  • Week 2 — Draft rules. Write principles, approved and prohibited uses, data rules and verification steps. Apply the legitimacy test to every approved use.
  • Week 3 — Build response capability. Draft the disinformation response plan, the truth-sandwich templates and the incident escalation chart; run a tabletop exercise with a fictional deepfake scenario.
  • Week 4 — Validate and present. Seek review from a legal adviser and a communications lead; finalise roles, training plan and review schedule.

Deliverables checklist.

  • ☐ Civic AI Playbook document
  • ☐ Legal and regulatory context table
  • ☐ Approved/prohibited uses matrix with the legitimacy test applied
  • ☐ Disinformation response plan with templates
  • ☐ Tabletop exercise report (scenario, decisions, lessons)
  • ☐ Training and review schedule

Assessment rubric (weighted).

  • Legal and democratic soundness — 25%: laws identified correctly; rights and integrity protected
  • Practical usability — 20%: clear rules and roles usable under pressure
  • Transparency and accountability — 15%: disclosure and responsibility well defined
  • Disinformation readiness — 20%: credible monitoring, verification and response
  • Evidence of testing — 10%: tabletop exercise and lessons applied
  • Presentation — 10%: concise and persuasive to decision-makers
Worked mini-example. A municipal council's communication unit in Cameroon adopts AI for drafting plain-language notices in French and English and for summarising public consultation comments. Red lines: no synthetic images of officials, no automated decisions on citizens' requests, and no uploading of citizens' personal data to unapproved tools. In the tabletop exercise, a fake audio clip of the mayor announcing a market closure circulates on WhatsApp; the team verifies with the mayor's office within an hour, posts a truth-sandwich correction through official channels and trusted community leaders, and logs the incident.

Common failure modes.

  • Copying a generic AI policy that ignores local electoral and data protection law.
  • No prohibited-uses list, so staff assume anything is allowed.
  • Disinformation plans that rely on one person being available.
  • Overclaiming detection tools as proof of whether content is synthetic.
  • No review date, despite rapidly changing laws and tools.

Submission and presentation structure.

  • 1. Mandate, context and risks
  • 2. Principles and the legitimacy test
  • 3. Approved and prohibited uses
  • 4. Disinformation response demonstration (tabletop results)
  • 5. Roles, training, review and the decisions requested
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

Act as a red-team facilitator for my civic organisation. Using my playbook summary [paste], design a 45-minute tabletop exercise: a realistic disinformation incident (e.g., a fake audio clip or doctored document) unfolding in three stages. For each stage, give the facts available, the decisions my team must take and the playbook sections they should use. End with debrief questions that expose gaps in our plan.

📚 Glossary

  • Civic AI playbook: practical guidance for responsible AI use in public life
  • Legitimacy test: whether full public knowledge of an AI use would increase or decrease trust
  • Response threshold: criteria for when to respond to false information

📖 References

  • OECD AI Principles; UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI.
  • International IDEA — AI and elections resources.
  • European Union — AI Act and political advertising regulation.
  • National data protection and electoral laws (verify for your country).

quiz.q: A Cameroonian NGO's playbook allows AI for 'all communications'. A reviewer says it is too broad. Which change best reflects the module?
opts: Restrict AI use to the director, who will approve every output personally
Specify the brand of AI tool that staff should use for communications
Add a sentence asking staff to use AI responsibly and follow the law
List approved uses like translation and casework, plus prohibited uses
quiz.x: The playbook needs approved uses and prohibited uses with red lines. Naming a tool helps data rules but does not define permitted uses.

quiz.q: A US city's playbook proposes AI-scored eligibility for housing vouchers with no human review. Applying the legitimacy test, what is the likely result?
opts: Likely lowers trust; redesign with legal basis and human checks
Passes, if residents are told decisions are automated in the notices
Likely increases trust, because automated decisions are more consistent
Passes, if the scoring model is audited for accuracy once per year
quiz.x: Automated decisions about citizens without legal basis and human review are listed as prohibited; public knowledge would likely decrease trust. Disclosure alone does not fix the lack of review.

quiz.q: A legislature office's playbook lacks any section on what to do when AI output contains an error that is published. Which component is missing?
opts: Training and review schedule
Approved uses and tools for each team
Context and jurisdiction
Verification, review and corrections
quiz.x: Verification and review includes sources for every fact, human review before publication and correction procedures. The training schedule concerns updating the playbook, not correcting errors.

quiz.q: A playbook's disinformation plan says 'respond to all false claims within one hour'. What is the main weakness?
opts: It does not name which AI tool will draft the responses
It should require legal approval before every response
It lacks response thresholds based on reach and harm
One hour is too slow for claims that spread on WhatsApp
quiz.x: Response thresholds define when to respond, so fringe claims are not amplified. Speed matters, but responding to everything is the core problem.

quiz.q: A playbook for a Kenyan county government needs a context section. Which content belongs there?
opts: Its mandate, audiences, jurisdiction and applicable laws
Templates for truth-sandwich corrections in Swahili and English
A list of AI tools and their licence costs for the coming year
The names of staff who review AI outputs before publication
quiz.x: Context covers organisation, mandate, audiences, jurisdiction and applicable laws. Staff names belong in roles and accountability.

quiz.q: A mentor reviews a campaign's playbook that allows AI-drafted attack ads based on 'likely' facts about the opponent. Which review criterion is most clearly failed?
opts: Brevity, because the playbook is limited to six pages in total
Democratic integrity and truthfulness, due to unverified claims
Non-partisanship, because the ads target a single opponent
Practicality, because the ads would take too long to verify
quiz.x: Unverified claims about opponents breach truthfulness and democratic integrity. Non-partisanship in review means applying the same standards, not banning contrast ads.

quiz.q: A Ugandan civic network has finished its AI playbook and asks its mentor how often it should be updated in the years ahead.
opts: On a set schedule, as laws and tools change, with staff training
Whenever the AI vendor releases a new version of its main model
When a serious incident occurs that involves the organisation
Once a year, timed to coincide with the organisation's budget cycle
quiz.x: Training and review should follow a schedule as laws and tools change. Incident-only updates are reactive.

quiz.q: A ministry's playbook says AI may analyse citizen feedback. Which data rule is most important to add?
opts: Publish the raw feedback so the analysis is fully transparent
Use a single AI tool so all analyses are consistent over time
Store all feedback indefinitely so trends can be compared over many years
Protect sensitive data and avoid profiling individuals' political opinions
quiz.x: Data rules should protect sensitive data and avoid profiling individuals for political opinions. Publishing raw feedback would breach privacy.

quiz.q: A civic organisation drafts a 14-page playbook. Its mentor asks for changes. What is most likely needed?
opts: Splitting it into two playbooks for staff and volunteers
Condensing to six pages or fewer, with practical, usable guidance
Adding an executive summary while keeping the full 14 pages
Adding more legal citations to support each of the principles
quiz.x: The capstone limits the playbook to six pages to keep it practical. An executive summary helps but does not meet the length limit.

quiz.q: A party office plans to disclose AI use only when asked. What is the main gap in its transparency section?
opts: It should require consent from voters before any AI use in campaigns
It should ban AI use in any communication that members of the public will read
It should state when and how AI use is disclosed to the public proactively
It should outsource disclosure decisions to the AI vendor's policy
quiz.x: Transparency components define when and how AI use is disclosed to the public. Banning AI use is excessive; consent from voters is impractical and not the requirement.

facts.t: Components in the civic AI playbook.
facts.more: Context, principles, approved uses, red lines, data rules, verification, transparency, disinformation response, roles and accountability, and training and review.

facts.t: Maximum length of the capstone playbook.
facts.more: Short enough that staff and volunteers actually use it. Add the disinformation template and one worked example.

facts.t: The legitimacy test: would full public knowledge of this AI use raise or lower trust?
facts.more: If the honest answer is 'lower', redesign the use or remove it, whether you are a ministry, a party or an NGO.

facts.t: Your mentor reviews legality, non-partisanship, practicality and democratic integrity.
facts.more: A playbook that only one side of politics could adopt fails non-partisanship.

labs.title: Which playbook component does this belong in?
labs.intro: Match each draft line to the playbook component it belongs in.
pairs: 'Constituent files only in the approved, encrypted tool'
'Every figure has a source; a second person reviews before posting'
'Respond publicly only if a claim reaches 5,000+ shares or risks safety'
'The chief of staff approves new AI uses'
'AI-assisted content is labelled on our website'
'Refresher session every six months as laws change'
labs.tip: A component without concrete rules is just a heading.

labs.title: Spot the problems in this draft playbook
labs.intro: An MP's office drafted this playbook excerpt with AI. Tap the lines that would fail mentor review.
segments: Purpose: help the office serve constituents faster and more accurately.
Approved uses: summarising bills, drafting casework letters and translating notices.
We may use AI to profile constituents by party sympathy to prioritise casework.
Profiling by political opinion is unlawful in many systems and fails equality and the legitimacy test.
All published facts must have a source, and staff review every output.
Rival parties' statements may be paraphrased by AI and attributed as quotes.
Fabricated quotes break the truthfulness red line.
AI use is never disclosed, to avoid confusing the public.
Transparency is a core component. Hiding AI use lowers trust.
Incidents are reported to the chief of staff within 24 hours.
The playbook is final and needs no review.
Laws and tools change. A review schedule is a required component.
labs.tip: Check every line against legality, truthfulness, transparency and the legitimacy test.

plaibox.title: Civic AI playbook builder
plaibox.intro: Assemble a prompt to draft your playbook. Paste it into your AI tool, then review each component against the legitimacy test yourself.
